narrative.overview:
Every screen in kakapo reads like a short report from someone who has just checked the server: the verdict first, in one plain sentence, then why it matters, then what to do, then the evidence in small print. A consultant who is not a SQL specialist should get the answer from the first line, and be able to hand the whole report to IT as it stands. The interface is the paper the report is written on; it does not compete with what the report says.

The look is calm and friendly. It is a neutral, grey shadcn interface (Geist, small type, white or near-black surfaces that follow the operating system's theme) where colour is spent almost entirely on status. Calm means nothing shouts until it needs to: a healthy database is mostly grey text with a few green dots. Friendly means sentences, not codes, lead; numbers and identifiers follow in a quieter voice. Density is that of a well-set report, not a console: one column of cards and findings at most 72rem wide, with room between them.

kakapo must never look like a DBA console (grids and DMV columns first, sentences never), a monitoring dashboard (gauges, big charts, walls of red and green tiles), or a marketing site (hero gradients, display type, illustrations, glossy cards).
keyCharacteristics: A sentence leads every card, finding and dialog; the numbers come after it, smaller and greyer.
Neutral greys everywhere; red, amber and green carry status and nothing else.
Flat surfaces separated by hairlines and a faint ring, never by shadows.
Literal values (hosts, builds, paths, SQL) are set in monospace and can be copied.
Light and dark both, following the operating system.

rules.name: The One Meaning Rule
rules.body: Red is act today, amber is something to do, green is no problem found, grey is not checked. A colour never decorates, and never means two things.

rules.name: The Grey Default Rule
rules.body: A screen with nothing wrong is almost entirely grey and black. If a healthy page looks colourful, something is spending status colour on decoration.

rules.name: The Sentence-First Rule
rules.body: The first line of any card, finding or dialog is a sentence in Body or larger; the evidence under it is Label size in Quiet Ink. Never lead with a number or a code.

rules.name: The Copyable Literal Rule
rules.body: Anything set in monospace is something the user may copy, and statement blocks carry their own Copy button.

rules.name: The No-Shadow Rule
rules.body: Surfaces never cast shadows at rest or on hover. If something needs to stand apart, use a ring, a hairline or a tint.

dos: Do open every card, finding and dialog with a plain sentence, then put numbers and identifiers under it in Label type and Quiet Ink.
Do keep status colour to its one meaning: red act today, amber to do, green no problem, grey not checked.
Do set hosts, build stamps, paths, SQL and commands in monospace, with a Copy button on statement blocks.
Do separate surfaces with the 10% ring, hairlines and the Quiet Surface tint.
Do support light and dark through the existing tokens, following the operating system's theme.
Do fold expert detail (plans, per-file tables, raw counters) under the answer instead of removing it.
Do lead a verdict with what it means and put SQL Server's own name in brackets after it, and put raw settings on a quieter line under a plain one.
Do say "Nothing to act on today" in grey when there are no red flags: never a green tick above cards that still have things to do.
donts: Don't make it look like a DBA console: no grid or DMV columns as the first thing on a screen.
Don't make it look like a monitoring dashboard: no gauges, no wall of red and green tiles, no auto-refreshing charts as the lead.
Don't make it look like a marketing site: no gradients, display type, illustrations or glossy cards.
Don't add shadows to cards, buttons or notices.
Don't use solid red or amber fills for whole blocks; status lives in text, dots, borders and light tints.
Don't introduce a second sans or a decorative typeface.
